title: Transposition of the great arteries and Jatene procedure: anatomy, neonate stabilization and coronary translocation
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 110 (Transposition of the Great Arteries)
Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery 4e Ch 44 (Complete Transposition of the Great Arteries)
Congenital Heart Surgery Nomenclature and Database Project: TGA

steps.say: Complete transposition of the great arteries features complete ventriculoarterial discordance with concordant atrioventricular connections. The aorta arises anteriorly from the morphological right ventricle, while the pulmonary artery arises posteriorly from the morphological left ventricle. This abnormal connection completely separates pulmonary and systemic circuits.
steps.tx: In complete **d-TGA**, cardiac anatomy exhibits concordant atrioventricular connections alongside complete **ventriculoarterial discordance**. The ascending aorta arises anteriorly from the **morphologic right ventricle**, while the main pulmonary trunk originates posteriorly from the morphologic left ventricle, establishing two isolated parallel vascular circuits.

steps.say: Because systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel, deoxygenated blood recirculates systemically while oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs. Immediate neonatal survival depends entirely on bidirectional mixing between the circuits. Mixing occurs through a patent ductus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, or ventricular septal defect.
steps.tx: Because the circulations operate in **parallel circulation** rather than normal series, oxygenated pulmonary venous blood cannot reach systemic tissues without **bidirectional mixing**. Extrauterine survival depends entirely on **ductal dependence** and interatrial communications (ASD or PFO) to allow reciprocal exchange of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

left.title: Normal Series Circulation
points: Systemic venous blood flows to right heart and lungs
Pulmonary venous blood flows to left heart and body
Zero mixing sites required for tissue oxygenation

right.title: Transposition Parallel Circulation
points: Deoxygenated systemic venous blood recirculates to aorta
Oxygenated pulmonary venous blood recirculates to lungs
Mandatory bidirectional shunt required across PDA, ASD, or VSD

steps.say: Initial medical stabilization begins immediately with intravenous prostaglandin E1. Infusion maintains ductal patency and prevents acute hypoxemic arrest. If severe cyanosis persists despite ductal opening, emergency balloon atrial septostomy by the Rashkind technique creates a non-restrictive atrial defect at the bedside.
steps.tx: Immediate medical stabilization requires continuous **prostaglandin E1** infusion to maintain ductal patency and systemic perfusion. If profound cyanosis persists with poor interatrial mixing, emergency **balloon atrial septostomy** using the **Rashkind procedure** is performed under ultrasound guidance to create an unrestrictive atrial communication.

nodes.label: Neonate presents with severe refractory cyanosis and d-TGA
Start continuous intravenous prostaglandin E1 immediately
Evaluate interatrial septum and mixing by echocardiography
Perform bedside balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure)

steps.say: The arterial switch operation, known as the Jatene procedure, is the definitive anatomical repair of choice. It must be performed within the first two to three weeks of life. Waiting longer allows left ventricular mass to regress as pulmonary resistance falls, leaving the ventricle unable to support systemic pressure.
steps.tx: The **arterial switch operation**, or **Jatene procedure**, is the gold standard anatomical repair. It must be completed within the critical **LV regression window** of 2 to 3 weeks of life. Beyond this window, dropping neonatal pulmonary vascular resistance causes left ventricular myocardial thinning and loss of systemic workload capacity.

rows: Thick-walled, conditioned LV at systemic pressure
Check LV geometry, mass, and septal shift on echo
Regressed, thin-walled LV with low mass
Requires LV retraining before arterial switch

steps.say: Coronary transfer is the most demanding technical step of the Jatene operation. Both coronary ostia are harvested with generous buttons of surrounding aortic wall. The surgeon carefully mobilizes and translocates these buttons into the neo-aortic root without twisting, kinking, or excessive tension.
steps.tx: The core technical challenge is **coronary button transfer**. Both coronary ostia are excised with wide patches of sinus tissue, meticulously mobilized, and implanted into medially placed neo-aortic trapdoors. Perfect **coronary translocation** into the **neoaorta** without torsion, kinking, or stretching is essential to prevent acute myocardial infarction.

left.title: Coronary Button Mobilization
points: Excise wide, generous cuffs of native aortic sinus tissue
Implant into neo-aortic root without kinking or rotation

right.title: Technical Pitfalls to Avoid
points: Geometric torsion or kinking during neo-aortic distension
Acute perioperative left ventricular ischemic collapse

steps.say: The LeCompte maneuver translocates the pulmonary bifurcation anterior to the reconstructed aorta. Before sewing the neo-pulmonary artery, the surgeon brings the pulmonary confluence forward across the neo-aorta. This maneuver relieves tension on the pulmonary branches and prevents extrinsic compression.
steps.tx: The **LeCompte maneuver** brings the bifurcated **pulmonary confluence** from its posterior origin across to an **anterior translocation** plane in front of the neo-aortic root. This anatomical rearrangement aligns the pulmonary artery branches naturally, eliminating stretch and minimizing postoperative branch pulmonary artery stenosis.

nodes.label: Transect great arteries above semilunar valve commissures
Mobilize distal pulmonary artery confluence and left/right branches
Pass pulmonary bifurcation anterior to the ascending neo-aorta
Construct neo-pulmonary anastomosis with autologous pericardial patch

steps.say: If an infant with intact ventricular septum presents late, the left ventricle requires retraining. Beyond three to four weeks of life, a regressed ventricle will fail if exposed immediately to systemic afterload. A two-stage approach uses pulmonary artery banding and a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt to rebuild muscle mass.
steps.tx: When an infant presents beyond 3 to 4 weeks of age with a **regressed left ventricle**, primary switch causes acute left heart failure. A staged strategy achieves **LV retraining** through initial **pulmonary artery banding** and a systemic-to-pulmonary modified Blalock-Taussig shunt, inducing pressure hypertrophy over 7 to 14 days prior to definitive arterial switch.

left.title: Stage 1: Rapid LV Retraining
points: Place pulmonary artery band to induce pressure overload
Add systemic-to-pulmonary shunt to ensure pulmonary flow
Monitor left ventricular mass index and septal shift on echo

right.title: Stage 2: Definitive Arterial Switch
points: Perform once LV mass index exceeds 35-50 g/m2
Remove PA band, take down shunt, and complete Jatene switch
Left ventricle successfully supports systemic circulation

steps.say: Congenitally corrected transposition features both atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Blood flows in the correct physiological direction, but the morphological right ventricle supports the systemic circulation. Long-term systemic right ventricular failure is treated with a double switch operation combining an atrial switch with an arterial switch.
steps.tx: In **congenitally corrected TGA**, physiological flow is preserved but the morphological right ventricle functions as the systemic pumping chamber. To prevent late right heart failure, anatomical repair is accomplished with the **double switch operation**, which unites an atrial switch (**Senning procedure** or Mustard) with a Jatene arterial switch.
